summary:
KwaZulu-Natal is a province of South Africa and stands under the national framework: the constitutional equality guarantee, the Equality Court under the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act, legal gender recognition, the 2024 hate-crime statute and the national correctional rules for transgender inmates apply here as they do elsewhere in the country. No provincial law, by-law or provincial institution departing from that layer is documented in the sources.

The provincial evidence on violence and victimisation is a 2024 masters thesis in criminology at the University of KwaZulu-Natal in Durban. It interviewed 15 self-identifying queer participants recruited through the Imvelo Yesizwe Organisation in KwaMashu township and reports substantial queerphobic violence and victimisation in that township setting. The study also examines whether the support and interventions available to those residents were adequate, and what safety strategies they used.

The study is small and its participants were purposively recruited, so it records the experiences of that group rather than a measured rate of violence. It does not disaggregate transgender participants from other sexual minorities, and no source gives a KwaZulu-Natal figure for violence against transgender people. A trans visitor to the province has no validated local victimisation figure to work from.
tangentialFactors:
The Zulu King Goodwill Zwelithini made anti-gay remarks at a harvest festival in January 2012, which drew demands for an apology; a police investigation was opened, and the then KwaZulu-Natal Premier and the Congress of Traditional Leaders of South Africa intervened over the royal family's account. The remarks concerned gay people rather than transgender people, carried no legal force, and are more than a decade old. No later statement from KwaZulu-Natal traditional leadership on transgender people appears in the sources.

Traditional authority in the province is a social influence on how gay and transgender people are treated locally rather than a source of enforceable rules, and nothing in the sources connects it to a specific enforcement practice against trans visitors.
localsOnly:
The KwaMashu research is resident-facing. It documents queerphobic victimisation among people living in the township and asks whether the interventions and support structures available to them, including through the Imvelo Yesizwe Organisation, actually met their needs and what safety strategies residents adopted.

No provincial department, provincial programme or provincial body directed at violence against transgender or LGBTI residents is documented for KwaZulu-Natal; the protection machinery appearing in these sources sits at the national level.
outOfScopeNotes:
Interview content, specific incidents and participant breakdowns from the KwaMashu thesis are not reproduced in the inventory, so it is unresolved how many participants were transgender and what incidents they described.

Whether and how the national correctional standards for transgender inmates are applied in KwaZulu-Natal facilities is not sourced, and no KwaZulu-Natal correctional complaint or case involving a transgender person appears.

Whether the police investigation opened after the January 2012 remarks by the Zulu King reached any outcome is not sourced, and no subsequent statement by KwaZulu-Natal traditional leadership on transgender people is recorded.

Police handling of complaints, identity-document problems when presentation and documents do not match, and gender-segregated facilities in KwaZulu-Natal specifically are not documented; the analyses addressing those points are national in scope.
